methods.label: Split along a shared base
methods.explanation:
The equality \(BF=AG\) is useful because these segments also lie on parallel sides of the parallelogram. Thus \(BF\parallel AG\), and quadrilateral \(ABFG\) has one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel. It is a parallelogram, so
\[
FG\parallel AB\qquad\text{and}\qquad FG=AB=3.
\]
Draw diagonal \(FG\) of the desired quadrilateral. It splits \(EFHG\) into triangles \(EFG\) and \(HFG\), both with base \(FG\).

Let \(h\) be the perpendicular distance between \(AB\) and \(CD\). Because \(FG\) lies between these parallel lines, the perpendicular distances from \(E\) and \(H\) to \(FG\), say \(h_1\) and \(h_2\), satisfy \(h_1+h_2=h\). Here we use only that \(E\) lies on \(AB\) and \(H\) lies on \(CD\); the exact position of \(H\) along \(CD\) is unnecessary.

The area of the original parallelogram gives \(3h=10\). Therefore
\[
[EFHG]=\frac12(3)h_1+\frac12(3)h_2
=\frac12(3h)=\boxed{5},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
